Senses.Explanation: The normal Chan use is a title for the person who teaches and presides over a monastic community. It follows a personal name in lineage headings, as in “Master Bodhidharma” (菩提達摩和尚), and opens biographies such as “Master Puhua of Zhenzhou, who ...” (鎮州普化和尚者). A student can state that he comes from Master An of Songshan, while lamp records quote an authority with “Master Wuzu Fayan said” (五祖演和尚曰). The title also marks institutional and public relations. The “master at the head of the hall” (堂頭和尚) is asked to address the assembled community; another monk asks the master to “speak the teaching for the assembly” (請和尚為眾說法). Direct address changes English capitalization and syntax but not the referent. Huike says, “I only beg you, Master, to show compassion” (惟願和尚慈悲); a monk asks the Cloth-Bag Monk, “Master, what are you doing here?” (和尚在這裏作甚麼); and a cloister director asks after the master's health before the reply “Sun-face Buddha, Moon-face Buddha.” A collective public saying can gather “all the old masters under heaven” (天下老和尚) in one place. Across these forms, the Chan deviation is institutional and documentary: the word identifies the named person questioned in encounters, invited to teach from the seat, cited in lineage, and quoted as the head of a community.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 52,209 occurrences in 441 texts. Render direct address as capitalized “Master”; in narrative prose use “the master,” a named form such as “Master Bodhidharma,” or “abbot” only where the office is explicit. Direct address is grammatical variation, not a separate sense. The embedded form “monk-fellows” (和尚子) is a separate compound. The ordination-preceptor role is separately attested below and must not be merged into this teaching relation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第二十八祖菩提達摩和尚三三〇第二十九祖師慧可禪師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Patriarchs' Hall Collection table of contents places the title after Bodhidharma's name: "the twenty-eighth patriarch, Master Bodhidharma."

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖憫而問曰。汝久立雪中。當求何事。光悲淚曰。惟願和尚慈悲。開甘露門。廣度羣品。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Compendium of the Five Lamps account, Huike directly addresses Bodhidharma: "I only beg you, Master, to show compassion."

Occurrences.Kwic: 師在街衢立，有僧問：和尚在這裏作甚麼？師曰：等箇人。曰：來也，來也。師曰：汝不是這箇人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Complete Book of the Five Lamps, a monk publicly asks the Cloth-Bag Monk, "Master, what are you doing here?" He replies, "Waiting for a person."

Occurrences.Kwic: 今五祖堂頭和尚，此日幸對人天廣眾，請不悋慈悲，重為顯揚，使先宗有據，吾道益明

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked where he comes from, the student says he comes from Master An of Songshan, anchoring teacher provenance.

Occurrences.Kwic: 院主問和尚近日尊候如何師曰日面佛月面佛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The cloister director asks after the master's health; the master replies, “Sun-face Buddha, Moon-face Buddha.”

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp biography opens with Master Puhua of Zhenzhou and identifies his teacher relation to Panshan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 天下老和尚緫在這裏我若放一線道從汝七縱八橫
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address gathers all the old masters under heaven “here,” a collective use of titled teaching figures.

Senses.Explanation: In ordination accounts the same title names the person from whom someone receives the precepts, a different office from the teaching master. Biographical sequences distinguish the roles explicitly: one nun "first shaved her head at Wanyuan Cloister, investigated under Guixi Zhuang, then received the precepts from Preceptor Baochi, and finally heard the teaching from Old Man Yi'an" (初披剃於萬緣寺，參學於桂谿莊，繼受戒於寶池和尚，終聞法於易菴老人). Another record separates "listening to the teaching under Teacher Buye" from "receiving the precepts from Preceptor Yulin" (聽教於不夜天師、受戒於玉林和尚). The office is also named directly: a woman asks "Preceptor Ruo'an of Louze to serve as the preceptor from whom she received the precepts" (乞漏澤箬菴和尚為得戒師), while incense verses honor a "preceptor from whom the precepts were received" (得戒和尚) alongside the distinct tonsure teachers. This is a precept-family deployment of the title: it identifies the human conferrer in an ordination relation, not merely a respectful reading of the teaching-master sense.
Senses.Note: Do not infer this sense from every occurrence of “precept/Master Jie” (戒和尚). In early lamp records that sequence often means “Master Jie,” where Jie is a personal name, especially Wuzu Jie. The verified line “arrived at Master Wuzu Jie” (到五祖戒和尚處) is a teacher-name use, not ordination. Assign the preceptor sense only when receiving or conferring precepts, the explicit title “preceptor from whom the precepts were received” (得戒和尚), or an equivalent role statement supplies the relation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 初披剃於萬緣寺，參學於桂谿莊，更歷寒暑，道念愈堅。繼受戒於寶池和尚，終聞法於易菴老人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The biography separates tonsure, investigation, receiving precepts from Preceptor Baochi, and finally hearing the teaching from Yi'an, making the ordination role explicit.

Occurrences.Kwic: 余挂錫半載，辭水月方丈，北遊燕山，聽教於不夜天師、受戒於玉林和尚。後住崇寧禪院
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker distinguishes "listening to the teaching under Teacher Buye" from "receiving the precepts from Preceptor Yulin."

Occurrences.Kwic: 復乞漏澤箬菴和尚為得戒師，是時余居三師之列。違今年已六十矣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record says that Preceptor Ruo'an of Louze was asked to serve explicitly as the "preceptor from whom the precepts were received."

Occurrences.Kwic: 此瓣香，分弗為兩，析不成三，爇向爐中，奉上高峰得戒和尚、薙髮二位尊師，伏願三聚嚴明
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An incense verse offers incense to the Gaofeng "preceptor from whom the precepts were received" and to two separate tonsure teachers.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, mixing (和) mud (泥) and blending (合) water (水): "mixing mud and blending water." The phrase occurs 343 times in 113 allowlisted texts. Chan records make the ordinary mixing image an appraisal of sayings, explanations, and speakers. In a recasting of three phrases, "understanding from the first phrase" is called "mixing mud and blending water," followed by "binding oneself without a rope" and "landing with all four edges on the ground" (第一句薦得，和泥合水；第二句薦得，無繩自縛；第三句薦得，四稜著地). Another record groups it with "speaking a dream without a dream" and "not knowing good from bad" (無夢說夢，和泥合水，撒屎撒尿，不識好惡). Yet the phrase also stands as a direct answer to "what is the true source of the great road?" (如何是大道真源), and one discourse pairs "where wind cannot enter" with "mixing mud and blending water" in both directions. Another contrasts failing to mark the moment, when black and white remain undistinguished, with marking it too late, called "mixing mud and blending water." These are different recorded placements of one image. The texts do not supply the uniform gloss “descending to the student's level,” so neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The phrase's evaluative direction varies with its sentence. Favorable and unfavorable modern readings are not separate lexical objects and are not split into senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第一句薦得，和泥合水；第二句薦得，無繩自縛；第三句薦得，四稜著地。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A three-part appraisal assigns mixing mud and water to understanding from the first phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 與麼說話，可謂無夢說夢，和泥合水，撒屎撒尿，不識好惡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is grouped with speaking a dream without a dream and not knowing good from bad.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：如何是大道真源？師云：和泥合水。僧云：便恁麼去時如何？師云：截斷草鞋跟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: It is the direct answer to "what is the true source of the great road?"

Occurrences.Kwic: 風吹不入處，和泥合水；和泥合水處，風吹不入。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The discourse pairs where wind cannot enter and mixing mud and water in a reciprocal formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 點時不到。皂白未分。到時不點。和泥合水。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is contrasted with failing to mark the moment while black and white remain undistinguished.

Senses.Explanation: Master Zhigong is the pre-Zen figure whom Chan records quote, identify with a direct answer, and place in exchanges at Emperor Wu's court. His name occurs 494 times in 133 allowlisted texts. Asked "what is buddha?" a master answers, "Master Zhigong" (誌公和尚); when challenged, he says, "Zhigong is not an idle monk" (誌公不是閑和尚). In the Fu Dashi case, Fu mounts the seat, strikes the desk once, and descends; Zhigong asks Emperor Wu whether he understands, then says, "the great man has finished lecturing the scripture" (大士講經竟). Later masters repeatedly quote and criticize that verdict. His sayings are also treated as named textual material: the Twelve-Hour Song, Fourteen Sections, and Great-Vehicle Praises. Zen therefore deploys Zhigong as a named answer to "what is buddha?," court interlocutor and adjudicator of Fu Dashi's action, and quoted author.
Senses.Note: One person sense. Zhigong (誌公), Master Zhigong (誌公和尚), and Baozhi (寶誌公) name the same figure in this corpus. Titles of works attributed to him are named works, not a second sense of the bare personal name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是佛。師曰。誌公和尚。曰。學人問佛。何故答誌公和尚。師曰。誌公不是閑和尚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master answers “what is buddha?” with Zhigong and defends the answer by saying Zhigong is not an idle monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 梁武帝請講金剛經，士纔陞座，以尺揮按一下，便下座，帝愕然。誌公曰：陛下會麼？帝曰：不會。誌公曰：大士講經竟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Fu Dashi case records Zhigong questioning Emperor Wu and declaring the lecture finished.

Occurrences.Kwic: 却被誌公云陛下還會麼。帝云。不會。誌公云。大士講經竟也。是一人作頭。一人作尾。誌公恁麼道。還夢見傅大士麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff commentary quotes Zhigong's verdict, calls the pair head and tail, and questions whether Zhigong even dreamed of Fu Dashi.

Occurrences.Kwic: 誌公和尚大乘讚十首誌公和尚十二時頌十二首誌公和尚十四科頌
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp-record contents section names three groups of works attributed to Zhigong.

Occurrences.Kwic: 誌公和尚云。內外追尋覔總無。境上施為渾大有。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master quotes Zhigong's contrast between finding nothing in inner and outer search and abundant activity on objects.

Occurrences.Kwic: 被誌公和尚一喝曰。大士莫作是說。別更道看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhigong shouts at Fu Dashi, rejects his first saying, and asks him to speak again.
